fragment: User is designing a system to verify authenticity of physical items by pairing each item with a Bitcoin Ordinal and embedding an NFC chip in the item. #ordinals-nfc #project

Proposed binding scheme for #ordinals-nfc: store the Ordinal's transaction ID on the NFC chip as the item's unique identifier, then verify by looking up that tx on the Bitcoin blockchain. #ordinals-nfc
Known weakness of the tx-ID scheme for #ordinals-nfc: Ordinal transaction IDs are public on-chain, so anyone could copy one onto a counterfeit NFC chip and fake authenticity. #ordinals-nfc #security

Mitigations recommended for #ordinals-nfc: concatenate tx ID with a random string/hash, use a per-item public-private key pair (public key in metadata, private key on chip), tamper-evident chips, holographic features, and multi-factor checks. #ordinals-nfc #security
Recommended NFC hardware for #ordinals-nfc: secure-element based chips such as NXP MIFARE DESFire EV3 and MIFARE SAM AV3. #nfc-hardware

Technical requirements for a secure NFC chip in #nfc-hardware: AES/RSA/ECC cryptography, secure key storage in the secure element, tamper sensors and side-channel countermeasures, secure channel protocol (SCP/TLS), per-application access keys, memory protection, and Common Criteria / FIPS 140-2/3 / EMVCo certification. #nfc-hardware

Bitcoin has no on-chain metadata like Ethereum, so for #ordinals-nfc the plan is off-chain JSON metadata (name, description, image, creator, unique_identifier, provenance) pinned to IPFS, with the IPFS hash linked to the Ordinal; RGB was mentioned as an option. #ordinals-nfc
The #ordinals-nfc discussion about combining Bitcoin Ordinals with NFC chips for physical-item authenticity took place on 2023/04/25. #ordinals-nfc

NFC chip crypto requirements for #nfc-hardware: AES/RSA/ECC support, secure key storage inside the secure element, tamper sensors plus side-channel countermeasures, and a secure channel protocol (SCP or TLS). #nfc-hardware
Certifications to require for a secure NFC chip in #nfc-hardware: Common Criteria (CC), FIPS 140-2/3, or EMVCo; also per-application access keys and memory protection/segmentation. #nfc-hardware

The Peshwas' revenue system was based primarily on land revenue and customs dues; taxes fell mainly on agriculture and trade, while artisan goods were mostly exempt. #PeshwaTaxation

Under the Peshwas, only land used to grow crops was considered revenue-yielding, and the cultivators working it were liable for tax. Land revenue was split into dry land (taxed at three-fourths of produce) and wetland (taxed at half of produce). #PeshwaTaxation
Besides land revenue, the Peshwas levied taxes on mines, trade routes, tolls and customs; merchants paid customs dues at the entrance of each port or city. #PeshwaTaxation
Peshwa taxes were collected by appointed revenue officials who were paid salaries and encouraged to collect efficiently and quickly. #PeshwaTaxation
Cultivators who failed to pay Peshwa taxes on time were fined, with the penalty varying by the unpaid amount and length of delay. #PeshwaTaxation
Continual non-payment under the Peshwas could lead to land confiscation and auction (the defaulter barred from bidding), imprisonment, and confiscation of property. #PeshwaTaxation
Peshwa revenue officials who failed to collect taxes on time were penalized, including deductions from their salaries. #PeshwaTaxation

The Peshwas encouraged timely tax payment by granting tax exemptions/rewards to cultivators who paid on time or in advance, and by offering low-interest loans to cultivators unable to pay. #PeshwaTaxation

Peshwa revenue officials were trained to deal with cultivators tactfully and visited villages to explain the benefits of paying taxes on time; officials who collected efficiently received bonuses and promotions. #PeshwaTaxation
